name: APOLLO
summary: The docked translunar stack: a command module for three, a service module carrying the engine that had to work twice, and a lunar module built so light its skin dented under a thumb. Flown in 1969; the real one is 17 m of vehicle for 6 m³ of living space.

rooms.name: Command Module Cabin
rooms.description: Six cubic metres of habitable volume for three men and ten days. Three couches lie abreast under a main display console of 24 instruments and 566 switches; the centre couch folds to open the lower equipment bay, where the guidance computer and the sextant live. The cabin flew at 34 kPa of pure oxygen. It is the only part of the stack that came home.

hotspots.title: Centre Couch
hotspots.text: Folds away to open the lower equipment bay and the sextant station.

hotspots.title: Main Display Console
hotspots.text: Twenty-four instruments and 566 switches across two metres of panel.

hotspots.title: Side Hatch
hotspots.text: Unified hatch, opened by a single handle in seven seconds after the 1967 fire.

rooms.name: Docking Tunnel
rooms.description: An 81 cm tunnel through the command module's apex with twelve latches around its rim. The probe and drogue at its mouth took the shock of docking, then came out by hand and stowed under a couch so the crew could float through to the lunar module. Transfer took about an hour, most of it spent stowing the hardware.

rooms.name: Service Propulsion System
rooms.description: One engine, 91 kN, with no backup and no ignition system: hypergolic propellants that burn on contact. It put the stack into lunar orbit and took it out again, and if it had failed at the second burn the crew would have stayed there. The nozzle is 2.1 m long and gimbals to track the shifting centre of mass.

rooms.name: Fuel Cells & Tanks
rooms.description: Three hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells making 1.4 kW each, plus the cryogenic tanks that feed them and the crew's drinking water as a by-product. Apollo 13's oxygen tank failed in this sector, which is why the service module is the part of the stack everyone can name. Radiators on the skin reject the heat.

rooms.name: High-Gain Antenna
rooms.description: Four 78 cm dishes on a deployable boom, steerable in two axes and pointed at Earth for the S-band link that carried voice, telemetry and television. At lunar distance it closed the link at a few watts. Folded against the service module for launch, it swung out after the panels came off.

rooms.name: Ascent Stage Cabin
rooms.description: Two men stood shoulder to shoulder for the descent: there are no seats, because standing saved weight and put their eyes at the triangular windows. Habitable volume is 4.5 m³. The skin is aluminium foil-thin in places, pressurised to 34 kPa, and the whole stage flew home on a single 15.6 kN engine that had to light the first time.

hotspots.title: Commander's Station
hotspots.text: Left position. Hand controller on the right, throttle on the left, window canted down 30°.

hotspots.title: Forward Hatch
hotspots.text: 81 × 81 cm, opened by depressurising the cabin. The crew went out backwards.

hotspots.title: Ascent Engine Cover
hotspots.text: The engine sits between the two crew; the cover doubles as a work surface.

rooms.name: Descent Stage
rooms.description: An octagonal box 4.27 m across carrying propellant, four landing legs, the throttleable descent engine and everything left on the Moon. Thrust ran from 4.7 to 45 kN, the first throttleable engine flown by a crew. Its skin is gold-tinted Kapton and aluminised Mylar, wrapped by hand for thermal control rather than looks.

rooms.name: Landing Gear
rooms.description: Four legs spanning 9.4 m between opposite footpads, with crushable aluminium honeycomb in the struts to absorb the touchdown. A 1.7 m contact probe hangs under three of the four pads; when one touched, a blue light told the crew to cut the engine. The ladder on the forward leg has nine rungs and ends a metre above the pad.

rooms.name: MESA Equipment Bay
rooms.description: The Modular Equipment Stowage Assembly: a quadrant of the descent stage that swings down on a lanyard to present the television camera, sample boxes, tools and the flag. It is the reason the first pictures from the surface exist — the camera watched the ladder as the commander came down it.

systems.name: Power
systems.description: Fuel cells in the service module run the whole stack until separation; the lunar module carries its own batteries once it undocks.

systems.name: Atmos
systems.description: Two separate oxygen loops at 34 kPa, joined only while the tunnel is open.

systems.name: Data
systems.description: Two guidance computers, one in each spacecraft, and one S-band link home.

segments.name: Docked Stack
segments.caption: Seventeen metres of spacecraft for six cubic metres of cabin. Three men, eight days, one engine that had to work twice.

segments.name: Service Module
segments.caption: Fuel cells, cryogenic tanks and the engine that put the stack into lunar orbit and took it out again.

segments.name: Command Module
segments.caption: Three couches abreast under 566 switches. The only part of the stack that came home.

segments.name: Docking Tunnel
segments.caption: Eighty-one centimetres, twelve latches, and an hour of stowing hardware to get through it.

segments.name: Ascent Stage
segments.caption: Two men standing at triangular windows, in a cabin whose skin dented under a thumb.

segments.name: Descent Stage
segments.caption: The first throttleable engine flown by a crew, under a box wrapped in gold Kapton by hand.

segments.name: Landing Gear
segments.caption: Nine and a half metres between footpads, with crushable honeycomb in every strut.

segments.name: Equipment Bay
segments.caption: The quadrant that swung down to reveal the camera that filmed the first step.
